entity.name: Thomas Edison
entity.description: The inventor who held 1,093 patents and expected 18-hour workdays. American creator of the phonograph, practical light bulb, and motion picture camera, Edison built the world's first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey. Nearly deaf from childhood, he listened to music by biting into the wood of a piano to feel vibrations through his skull.

story.name: Thomas Edison
story.description: Invents the phonograph and stuns the world, builds America's first research lab, lights up Manhattan with electricity, and wages a brutal "War of Currents" against Nikola Tesla. The Wizard of Menlo Park.

moments.name: Thomas Edison Is Born in Milan, Ohio, the Last of Seven Children
moments.subtitle: Mostly homeschooled and nearly deaf by 12, he will hold more patents than anyone in history
moments.description: On February 11, 1847, Thomas Alva Edison was born in Milan, Ohio, the seventh and last child of Samuel Edison Jr. and Nancy Matthews Elliott. The family moved to Port Huron, Michigan, in 1854. Edison attended school for only a few months before his mother, a former teacher, took over his education. By age 12, he developed severe hearing loss, likely from scarlet fever and untreated ear infections. Edison later claimed his deafness helped him concentrate, and he listened to music by clamping his teeth into wood to absorb sound vibrations through his skull.

moments.name: Edison Invents the Phonograph and Becomes the Wizard of Menlo Park
moments.subtitle: The machine that records and plays back human speech seems like pure magic to the public
moments.description: In 1877, Thomas Edison invented the phonograph at his laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey — the first device capable of recording and reproducing sound. The machine used a tinfoil-wrapped cylinder and a stylus that traced grooves corresponding to sound vibrations. When Edison demonstrated it publicly, audiences were stunned; the ability to capture a human voice seemed almost supernatural. In April 1878, Edison demonstrated the phonograph before the National Academy of Sciences. The invention earned Edison the nickname "The Wizard of Menlo Park" and made him one of the most famous people in the world.

moments.name: Edison Builds the World's First Industrial Research Laboratory
moments.subtitle: A factory for invention, stocked with 8,000 chemicals and shark teeth
moments.description: In 1876, Thomas Edison established the world's first industrial research laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey, funded by the sale of his quadruplex telegraph patent. Unlike individual workshops, this facility was designed for systematic, team-based invention. Edison drove his staff to work 18-hour days, six days a week. By 1887, the lab stocked 8,000 kinds of chemicals and an eccentric array of materials from ostrich feathers to shark teeth. The laboratory model Edison pioneered — organized R&D with dedicated staff — became the template for corporate research at Bell Labs, General Electric, and every major technology company that followed.
moments.address: Menlo Park, Edison Township, New Jersey

moments.name: Edison Flips the Switch on the First Commercial Power Station in Manhattan
moments.subtitle: 85 customers in lower Manhattan become the first people to receive centralized electric power
moments.description: On September 4, 1882, Thomas Edison activated the Pearl Street Station in lower Manhattan, the world's first commercial central power plant. The coal-fired station initially served 85 customers, including the offices of J.P. Morgan and The New York Times, powering about 400 electric lamps across a one-square-mile area. Edison's system used direct current (DC), which could only travel short distances — a limitation that would later fuel the bitter "War of Currents" with George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla's alternating current (AC) system. The Pearl Street Station proved that electricity could be commercially distributed to urban customers.

moments.name: Edison Dies at 84 in West Orange, Holding 1,093 U.S. Patents
moments.subtitle: President Hoover asks Americans to dim their lights for one minute in tribute
moments.description: On October 18, 1931, Thomas Edison died at his estate, Glenmont, in West Orange, New Jersey, at the age of 84. He held 1,093 U.S. patents — still one of the largest portfolios in history — covering the phonograph, motion picture camera, alkaline storage battery, and improvements to the electric light bulb and telephone. President Herbert Hoover suggested that Americans turn off their electric lights for one minute as a tribute, though the idea was ultimately deemed too disruptive. Edison's last breath was reportedly captured in a test tube by his son Charles, which Henry Ford later kept as a memento of his close friend.
moments.address: Glenmont Estate, West Orange, New Jersey
